questions.question: A developer selects the applyDiscount function in Visual Studio Code and wants GitHub Copilot to generate tests for it. Which Copilot Chat slash command should the developer use?

options.text: /tests
options.why: Correct. /tests generates tests for the selected code.

options.text: /fix
options.why: /fix proposes fixes for problems in the selected code.

options.text: /new
options.why: /new scaffolds a new project or file.

options.text: /clear
options.why: /clear clears the chat conversation.

questions.explanation: Use /tests and list the edge cases that the tests must cover.

questions.question: GitHub Copilot generates unit tests for a discount function. Two of the tests fail because the function returns NaN for an unknown discount code instead of the original total. What should the developer do?

options.text: Determine whether the function or the test is wrong, then fix the function if it does not meet the requirement and keep the test
options.why: Correct. A failing generated test can reveal a real defect and must be investigated.

options.text: Delete the failing tests because Copilot generated them
options.why: Deleting the tests discards evidence of a possible defect.

options.text: Change the assertions to check only that a value is returned
options.why: Weakening the assertions hides the defect instead of fixing it.

options.text: Regenerate the tests until all of them pass
options.why: Regenerating until tests pass can remove the test that detects the defect.

questions.explanation: Investigate failing tests. Here the function is wrong, so fix it and keep the test.

questions.question: A developer asks GitHub Copilot to identify edge cases for the function applyDiscount(total, code). Which TWO inputs are edge cases?

options.text: A discount code that does not exist
options.why: Correct. Unknown input is a common source of defects.

options.text: A call with no discount code
options.why: Correct. Missing input must be handled explicitly.

options.text: A total of 100 with the valid code SAVE10
options.why: This is a typical case within the normal range.

options.text: A total of 200 with the valid code HALF
options.why: This is a typical case within the normal range.

questions.explanation: Edge cases include unknown, missing, zero, boundary and very large values.

questions.question: Unit tests for the cart and discount modules pass. However, the checkout API in a test environment returns an incorrect total. Which type of test should the developer ask GitHub Copilot to generate to detect this problem?

options.text: An integration test that sends a request to the checkout endpoint and verifies the status code and total
options.why: Correct. Integration tests verify that the route and modules work together.

options.text: An additional unit test for the discount module with a mocked cart
options.why: Unit tests isolate components and may not detect problems in how they are connected.

options.text: A test that asserts only that the response body is defined
options.why: This assertion is too weak to detect an incorrect total.

options.text: A performance test that measures response time
options.why: Response time does not verify that the total is correct.

questions.explanation: Integration tests exercise several components together, such as an HTTP route and business logic.

questions.question: A developer reviews tests generated by GitHub Copilot. Which assertion most effectively verifies that the SAVE10 code applies a 10 percent discount to a total of 100?

options.text: assert.equal(applyDiscount(100, 'SAVE10'), 90)
options.why: Correct. It compares the result with an exact expected value for one behavior.

options.text: assert.ok(applyDiscount(100, 'SAVE10'))
options.why: This passes for any truthy value, including an incorrect total.

options.text: assert.doesNotThrow(() => applyDiscount(100, 'SAVE10'))
options.why: This confirms only that no exception occurs.

options.text: assert.notEqual(applyDiscount(100, 'SAVE10'), undefined)
options.why: This confirms only that a value is returned.

questions.explanation: Strong assertions check an exact expected value so that incorrect logic causes the test to fail.
